r: The applied work is elementary digital literacy: using email, retrieving online documents and software, operating a browser to search the web, and constructing basic web pages. The only thing slowing full realization at 24 months is that some students still enroll for the credential and hands-on familiarity, not any binding institutional or verification constraint. With no protective factor present, the instrumental need is already substantially eroded. Rating Medium, and only because credential adoption lags the trivially automated tasks.

By 2031 the tasks this course teaches (web navigation, file retrieval, email, basic web authoring) will be even more thoroughly absorbed into AI assistants that build pages, manage inboxes, and fetch resources on request. Absent any accreditation, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding constraint, nothing arrests the erosion. The honest hedge is that the course may persist for the least digitally prepared students as remediation, but the instrumental need (that a student must take it because the underlying work is not otherwise done) is largely gone. A decade out, the premise of a course teaching people to use email and browsers reads as anachronistic; AI systems will conduct search, retrieval, and web construction end-to-end, and web authoring in particular is squarely in the positively-exposed programming category identified by task-exposure research. The wide-uncertainty caveat here is not about capability, which is not in doubt for tasks this basic, but about whether such a course still exists in the catalog at all. If it does, it will be as digital-inclusion remediation for a shrinking population, not because the described work requires human execution. No verification, embodiment, foundational, or institutional factor protects it. I resist a confident point-prediction about curricular survival, but on the rating question of whether AI eliminates the instrumental need for the work, the 2036 answer is essentially yes. Rating High.
CSS 1080.d: This course is for anyone who uses or wants to access the World Wide Web or use the Internet. Students will master a set of basic skills including using electronic mail, logging in to remote computers, obtaining online documents and software, and using a browser like Netscape to search and explore the World Wide Web for information. Students will also learn the fundamentals of Web page construction.

By 2031 AI coding assistants will handle essentially all introductory VB implementation, and the rationale for a student to hand-author GUI event handlers weakens sharply. CSS 1247.d: This is an introductory computer programming course in which the major elements of Visual Basic are taught. Visual Basic is one of Microsoft's versions of Basic and was created to specialize in easy graphical user interface development. It is an object-based programming language with many characteristics of object oriented programming languages. Students will write programs to solve problems selected from a variety of applications.

CSS 1510.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 3 to 4. First programming course in FORTRAN whose outcome is writing and debugging routine programs. CSS 1510.d: This is a first course in computer programming for students in mathematics, science, or engineering, using the FORTRAN language. It includes an introduction to computer applications, program design, testing and debugging.

r: The applied work is foundational cybersecurity: understanding how computers and networks are attacked, how attackers benefit, and how to mitigate attacks, plus social engineering, cryptography, and application security. These map to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information, Identifying Objects/Actions/Events, and Making Decisions and Solving Problems activities. Security is adversarial and high-stakes: a plausible-looking but wrong mitigation invites breach, and failures are non-obvious, the jagged-frontier condition where AI users can be markedly less accurate with miscalibrated trust. That verification burden is the binding constraint, and it means oversight still requires a human holding this knowledge even where AI drafts configurations or summarizes threats. The course is also foundational scaffolding for the cybersecurity sequence, a prerequisite for the network, host, application, and forensics courses. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this conceptual security literacy is little eroded; AI assists analysis, it does not own the adversarial judgment. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI security tools (automated triage, threat summarization, control recommendation) will be more capable and widely deployed, meaningfully augmenting analysts. But the adversarial core keeps a knowledgeable human necessary: attackers actively adapt to defensive automation, and the cost of a missed or mis-scoped mitigation is severe and non-obvious, sustaining a high verification burden. Observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical work is the largest AI-use category, so exposure of the routine analytical layer is real, but exposure is not substitution where the failure mode is a live adversary. As foundational scaffolding for the security sequence, the course's erosion is further capped. The instrumental case shifts toward directing and validating AI-assisted defense rather than away from requiring the knowledge. The hedge: routine detection automates faster than expected, thinning entry-level roles, but the conceptual literacy remains needed for oversight. Rating Medium.

A decade out, AI will absorb much routine security operations (log analysis, alert triage, first-draft incident response), and defensive automation will be pervasive. Yet the adversarial, high-stakes nature of security means the verification burden does not disappear: an attacker's whole objective is to defeat automated defenses in non-obvious ways, and the jagged-frontier problem is acute where trust must be calibrated against an intelligent opponent. The foundational role for the security curriculum persists absent restructuring. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the operational shell automates around a still-human judgment core, not whether foundational security literacy remains instrumentally needed. I avoid a confident 2036 point-prediction on the security-labor market, which could contract at the routine tier. But the binding constraints, verification burden and foundational scaffolding, hold the rating at Medium rather than High. Rating Medium.
CSS 2751.d: This course provides a broad overview of cybersecurity. The terminology, approaches, and underlying technologies used in cybersecurity are covered. How computers and networks are attacked, how the attackers benefit, and how to mitigate attacks are addressed. Social engineering, cryptography, and application security are introduced.

By 2031, AI will draft policies, map controls to frameworks, and generate risk assessments with facility, offloading much documentation labor. That augments the assurance professional; it does not assume the accountable judgment about acceptable organizational risk, which carries legal and regulatory weight and non-obvious failure modes, a genuine verification burden. Task-exposure research classifies writing as strongly positively associated with exposure, so the drafting layer erodes, but assurance is judgment-and-accountability work, not merely document production. Foundational scaffolding for the security sequence further caps erosion. The instrumental case shifts toward directing and critically reviewing AI-generated governance artifacts rather than away from requiring the risk-reasoning competence. The hedge: standardized compliance drafting may automate substantially, thinning some GRC tasks, but the strategic and accountable core the course teaches remains necessary for oversight. Rating Medium.

A decade out, AI will routinely produce compliance documentation, risk registers, and control mappings, and much of the assurance paperwork will be automated. But the accountable judgment at the center (deciding what organizational risk is acceptable given legal, regulatory, and national-security stakes) retains a high verification burden, because errors are consequential and non-obvious and responsibility cannot be delegated to a model. The foundational role for the security curriculum persists. The real uncertainty is how much of the documentation shell automates around a still-human governance core, not whether foundational assurance literacy remains instrumentally required. I decline a confident 2036 claim about GRC staffing levels, which may compress at the routine tier. But verification burden and foundational scaffolding together hold the rating at Medium rather than High. Rating Medium.
CSS 2752.d: This course takes a broad, practical view of security - including people, policies and procedures, and technology. While Information Assurance (IA) encompasses the various technologies, it puts them in the context of an organization's overall strategy. It applies risk management techniques to cybersecurity risks. It includes addressing data both at rest and in transit. IA looks at many aspects of an organization's functioning including its legal, regulatory, and national security aspects.

CSS 2753.d: This class provides an overview of network security including threat models, web and electronic mail security, network layer security, transport layer security, packet filtering, firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention, and virtual private networks. Both wired and wireless security are covered. Methods for privacy and anonymity are discussed.

At 24 months the instrumental need to configure and verify host protections is little eroded; AI assists routine hardening, not the judgment about whether a system is actually secure. Rating Low.

The instrumental case shifts toward supervising AI-driven host defense rather than away from requiring the knowledge. A decade out, endpoint defense will be heavily automated (self-hardening systems, autonomous malware response, AI-managed backups), and much routine host administration absorbed. Yet the adversarial nature endures: attackers design to evade automated defenses in non-obvious ways, so calibrated human oversight of host-security posture remains necessary, and the verification burden does not vanish. Rating Medium.
CSS 2754.d: This course introduces the means for keeping computers safe. The topics of intrusion detection and protection, protection mechanisms, and auditing are introduced. Specific approaches to anti-virus and -malware protection are discussed. The importance of business continuity including secure backups are covered. More advanced protection mechanisms such as SELinux, AppArmor, EMET, multi-factor authentication, and least privilege are included.

CSS 3000.d: This course provides a broad overview of computing topics important to all Advanced Manufacturing disciplines. These topics include: algorithms and algorithmic thinking; computer programming; developing software to control robots and perform simulations; fundamental concepts in computer systems, networking, and hardware; human-computer interaction; legal, social and ethical implications of computing; and computer and data security.

r: The applied work is application security: understanding how applications are compromised and writing code across several languages and platforms so it resists compromise, secure development and code review. Coding is the most-exposed task class (GitHub Copilot showed roughly 55.8% speedups; the largest observed-usage category), and AI both writes and scans code for vulnerabilities. But the binding constraint is adversarial verification: a plausible-looking secure implementation that is actually exploitable fails non-obviously and catastrophically, precisely the jagged-frontier condition where AI users are markedly less accurate with miscalibrated trust. Oversight requires a human who understands the vulnerability. At 24 months the instrumental need to reason about application compromise is little eroded even as AI accelerates the coding; verifying security is exactly what the course builds. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will generate application code and flag many vulnerability classes automatically, offloading substantial secure-development labor. Coding's high exposure pushes the routine execution down, but security judgment is the residue the course centers. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying, reviewing, and adversarially testing AI-written applications rather than away from requiring the knowledge. The hedge: automated vulnerability detection may mature faster than expected for common bug classes, thinning routine review, but novel and logic-level flaws still demand human security reasoning. Rating Medium.

A decade out, AI will write much application code and catch many standard vulnerabilities, and routine secure-coding execution will be heavily automated. But application security is adversarial by construction: attackers design exploits that defeat automated defenses in non-obvious ways, so the verification burden endures, and human security reasoning remains necessary to specify, audit, and stress AI-generated software. The genuine uncertainty is how much routine hardening and scanning automate around a still-human adversarial-judgment core, not whether application-security competence remains instrumentally required. I decline a confident 2036 claim about secure-development staffing, which may compress for routine work as scanners improve. But the binding constraint, adversarial verification burden, holds the rating at Medium rather than High, even against coding's high exposure: the course teaches how applications are compromised across several platforms, so its value migrates toward threat modeling and reviewing AI-written code for the exploitable flaws automated tools miss, a competence that grows more necessary as more code is machine-generated. Rating Medium.
CSS 3751.d: Writing applications so that they are less susceptible to compromise is a critical aspect of cybersecurity. This course explores how applications are compromised and the steps that must be taken to make them more secure. Several different languages and platforms are covered.

r: The applied work is computer forensics: identifying and analyzing evidence types, low-level device analysis of filesystems, flash memory, and mobile devices, maintaining chain of custody, protecting evidence, and knowing when to involve law enforcement. These map to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information, Documenting/Recording Information, and Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance activities. Automated data recovery, log parsing, and artifact carving are exposed, but the binding constraint is a legal-verification burden: forensic conclusions must survive courtroom challenge, chain of custody is adversarially contested, and errors carry liberty-and-safety consequences that are non-obvious. The work is also partly embodied, involving physical seizure and low-level device handling. At 24 months the instrumental need for defensible forensic judgment is little eroded; AI accelerates artifact analysis, but the courtroom-defensible reasoning and evidentiary discipline the course builds are exactly what cannot be delegated. Rating Low.

By 2031, forensic tooling (automated artifact extraction, timeline reconstruction, cross-device correlation) will be more capable, meaningfully augmenting investigators. But the adversarial legal context is the binding constraint: evidence must withstand cross-examination, opposing counsel challenges every inference, and a flawed conclusion is costly and non-obvious, sustaining a high verification burden that keeps the trained human necessary. The partial embodiment of device handling further resists substitution. Observed-usage data shows analytical computing work is heavily represented in AI use, so the processing layer is exposed, but exposure is not substitution where admissibility and legal defensibility govern. The instrumental case shifts toward directing and validating AI-assisted analysis rather than away from requiring the competence. The hedge: routine data recovery and artifact carving automate over this horizon, so the descriptive layer thins. But the evidentiary judgment (establishing what an artifact proves, documenting chain of custody defensibly, deciding when to involve law enforcement) does not, because those are the parts a court and opposing counsel actually test. Rating Low.

A decade out, much forensic processing (carving, parsing, correlation across devices) will be heavily automated, and AI will surface candidate findings routinely. Yet the legal system's verification demands do not disappear: evidence must remain courtroom-defensible, chain of custody adversarially sound, and a conclusion that cannot survive cross-examination is worthless regardless of how it was produced. That binding constraint, plus the partly embodied device work, keeps human forensic judgment necessary, though the rising automation of pure analysis finally lifts base exposure enough to reach Medium by 2036. The genuine uncertainty is how much processing automates around a still-human evidentiary core, not whether defensible forensic reasoning remains instrumentally needed. I offer no confident 2036 claim about forensic staffing. Rating Medium, up from Low as routine analysis automates while legal verification holds.
CSS 3752.d: Once a cybersecurity incident has occurred, it must be investigated and reported so that an organization can learn from the incident. This course discusses the various types of evidence, how to analyze that evidence, and when to involve law enforcement. This course includes low-level device analysis including filesystems, flash memory, and mobile devices. The concepts of chain of custody and the protection of evidence while performing effective forensics are covered.

CSS 3753.d: As all aspects of manufacturing have become computerized, it is important that everyone involved become knowledgeable in computing in general and computer security specifically. This course gives a overview of what computing is and how programming is done. It covers how computers are connected to networks and the related networking protocols. It emphasizes manufacturing-specific concerns such as Industrial Control Systems and the Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) technology, protecting intellectual property at all phases, and assuring the software supply chain.
